text: Below root sits the identity you'll actually use every day: the IAM user. This lesson covers the three building blocks of AWS access control — individual users, the groups that organize them, and the policy documents that spell out exactly what each one can do.

An IAM user is a single named identity — one person, or sometimes one application — that can get its own console password, its own access keys, or both. Unlike root, a brand-new IAM user starts with zero permissions; it can't do anything until you grant it access. Giving every new hire a separate copy of the same permissions gets tedious and drifts over time, so IAM groups exist instead: a named collection of users that all inherit whatever policies are attached to the group itself. Add someone to the right group and they're fully provisioned in one step.

Users and groups both get their actual permissions from IAM policies — JSON documents built from statements. This one allows the s3:GetObject action on exactly one bucket, ltv-reports-bucket, and nothing else. Attach it to a Reporting-Readonly group and every member can download files from that bucket and nothing more.

Every statement has at least three parts. Effect is either Allow or Deny. Action names which API operations the statement covers. Resource names exactly which AWS resource it applies to, usually as an ARN. By default an identity with no attached policy can do nothing at all — access is implicitly denied — so a policy's job is to explicitly Allow specific actions on specific resources. When an Allow and a Deny both apply to the same request, Deny always wins, regardless of which policy it came from. That's the principle of least privilege in practice: exactly the access the job requires, never a convenient superset of it.

Users, groups, and policies cover identities created inside your own account. Next, Lesson 3 looks at IAM roles — temporary credentials assumed by a user, an application, or an AWS service itself, and why they're the safer alternative to long-lived access keys.
